classification.difficultyReason: Use labelled lengths to select the longest side and test the converse by comparing squared values, rather than relying on the triangles' appearance.

content.prompt: Which of the triangles below are right-angled triangles?

spec.description: Unshaded triangle with A below C and B to the right of A; no right-angle marker. Ordinary source blue strokes become black.
spec.mathematics: AB=2, AC=3, BC=4. Diagram appearance does not establish perpendicularity.
spec.answerVisibility: All vertex names and side lengths are permanent givens; no answer marks.

answer.worked:
The longest side is $BC=4$.
$$\begin{align*}AB^2+AC^2&=2^2+3^2\\AB^2+AC^2&=4+9\\AB^2+AC^2&=13\\BC^2&=4^2=16\end{align*}$$
Since $13\ne16$, the triangle is not right-angled.

spec.description: Unshaded triangle with A below C and B to the right of A; no right-angle marker. Ordinary source blue strokes become black.

answer.worked:
The longest side is $BC=13$.
$$\begin{align*}AB^2+AC^2&=5^2+12^2\\AB^2+AC^2&=25+144\\AB^2+AC^2&=169\\BC^2&=13^2=169\end{align*}$$
Since $AB^2+AC^2=BC^2$, the converse of Pythagoras’ theorem shows that the triangle is right-angled at $A$.
